screens.title: Test-Driven Design: Driving API and Class Structure
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll discover how test-driven development becomes a design discipline rather than only a verification tool. By writing tests first, you think like a client: you define how code must behave before choosing internal structures. This outside-in stance forces you to name methods, define parameters, and specify return values in ways that are intuitive for future users of the code. We'll follow concrete examples, including an OrderProcessor that starts as a failing test, moves to a minimal implementation, and then evolves through intentional refactoring. You'll see how each failing test reveals necessary dependencies, constructor shape, and interactions with collaborators such as payment or inventory services. Beyond a single example, we'll explore emergent design: how small tests lead to new classes or abstractions only when truly needed. We'll also highlight common pitfalls like testing implementation details or skipping refactoring, and explain why avoiding those mistakes matters. Finally, a hands-on activity will guide you to design a NotificationService via Red-Green-Refactor, so you can practice letting tests drive your A P I decisions. By the end you should be able to let tests safely steer A P I and class structure without over-design. What design question will your first test force you to answer?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how writing tests first shapes APIs and class structures. This includes describing outside-in design: starting from the client’s view of behavior and letting tests name methods and parameters. You will also identify opportunities for emergent design: recognizing when a raw data structure should become a domain object or when a new collaborator is needed. Finally, you will understand the role of refactoring backed by tests: why it is the phase where structural quality improves and how tests provide the safety net to evolve code without fear of regression. Each objective pairs a skill with a practical reason why it matters in real projects, and you will practice these skills in a guided activity to solidify the learning.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Practice
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives emphasize practice and judgment. First, you will write tests that act like a first consumer of your code. That habit forces A P I design decisions you would otherwise leave unexamined. As you add tests, you'll learn to notice when a simple function needs to become a small domain object or when two responsibilities should split into separate classes. Third, you'll practice constructor injection and collaboration through mockable dependencies so that your class boundaries are explicit and testable. Finally, you will adopt disciplined refactoring: after making a test pass you will improve names, extract classes, and remove duplication with confidence because the tests verify external behavior. Each objective ties directly to a short hands-on task where you write failing tests, implement minimal code, and refactor under test coverage so you leave the chapter with both knowledge and muscle memory.

screens.title: TDD as a Design Discipline
screens.narratorSegment: Test-driven development is often presented as a testing technique, but its deeper value is as a design discipline. The central claim is simple: when you write a test before code, you are forced to think about the desired behavior from the consumer’s perspective. That consumer view clarifies what methods should be named, which parameters are necessary, and what a sensible return value looks like. For example, a test that calls process_order forces you to design an OrderProcessor class and to decide whether the class should accept dependencies via its constructor. That single choice already separates concerns: payment and inventory interactions become collaborators rather than hidden internals. A common misconception is that tests only verify correctness; in practice, they reveal A P I shape and surface design smells early. Tests that are hard to write often indicate awkward APIs, which suggests a need to redesign for usability. To practice this definition, treat tests as client code: write them in a way you would like other engineers to call your A P I. A good closing question is: what client behaviors should your next test make obvious?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › TDD as a Design Discipline
Definition

Tests-first drives design

When tests are written first they act like the first consumer, revealing how the public API should look and what collaborators are needed.

Concrete example
A test that calls process_order suggests an OrderProcessor class and a constructor accepting payment and inventory services.
Common misconception
Tests are only for verification. In truth, they reveal API awkwardness and guide design changes early.
Key Takeaway

Treat tests as the first client; let them force API clarity before you implement internals.

Analogy
Think of tests as a contract from a future colleague. The clearer the contract, the easier the implementation and maintenance.
Check your understanding
Question
If a test is difficult to write, what does that usually indicate about the API?
Answer hint
It likely indicates the API is awkward or poorly named and needs redesign for clearer usage.

screens.title: Outside-In Design with TDD
screens.narratorSegment: Outside-in design is the habit of starting from observable behavior and working inward toward implementation. In TDD, the red test is the outside voice: it says what it expects from the system. By asking "How would I use this?" you force decisions about public A P I shape. For instance, choosing whether OrderProcessor accepts raw dictionaries or an Order object, or whether dependencies are passed in the constructor, is prompted by the test. A concrete example: your first failing test might construct OrderProcessor with two mocks and call process_order. That test establishes the constructor signature and the method name before any implementation exists. A common misconception is to assume outside-in prevents low-level design; instead it delays those details until the tests indicate them. The practical result is smaller, more focused classes, and clearer responsibilities. As you add failing tests one by one, the A P I stabilizes and you gain a roadmap for refactoring. Close with this reflection: what minimal A P I would your next test require? Outside-In Design with TDD means let failing tests dictate constructor and method signatures so the api matches how it will be used.. In practical terms, how tests act as the first clients and guide constructor and api choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Outside-In Design
Process

Red test defines external behavior

Follow a small sequence to let the API emerge:
1
Write a failing test
Act like a client and call the method you expect to exist; this forces names and signatures.
2
Implement minimal code
Add just enough to pass the test; keep internals simple and explicit.
3
Refactor thoughtfully
Now improve names and extract classes guided by passing tests.
Practical tip

If a test requires awkward arrangements, change the API until writing the test feels natural. Tests should be readable client examples.

Concrete scenario
Scenario: OrderProcessor
A failing test instantiates OrderProcessor with mock payment and inventory services and calls process_order. That test fixes the constructor signature and the method name before any implementation.
Misconception check
Outside-in does not forbid planning; it prioritizes immediate client needs and delays internal details until the tests demand them.

screens.title: Writing the First Failing Test
screens.narratorSegment: The Red phase begins by writing a test that fails because the targeted code doesn't exist yet. This test is a specification: it names the class, its constructor, and the method signature you expect. In our OrderProcessor example the test imports OrderProcessor before the class exists, constructs it with mocked payment and inventory services, calls process_order, and asserts on returned confirmation and collaborator interactions. This forces several design decisions at once: do you accept dependencies in the constructor? What should process_order accept and return? Do collaborators expose methods like charge and deduct_stock? A concrete walkthrough helps: the test asserts that payment_gateway. charge is called with the total amount and that inventory_service. deduct_stock is called per item. A common mistake is asserting internal state instead of observable interactions; prefer asserting the outputs and collaborator calls. The closing reflection is: which constructor arguments does your next red test force you to add? Writing the First Failing Test means write failing tests that name classes, constructors, methods, and expected collaborator interactions.. In practical terms, a test forces class existence, constructor shape, and interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Red Phase — Test
Code example
# test_order_processor.py
import pytest
from order_processor import OrderProcessor  # class not implemented yet
from unittest.mock import Mock

def test_process_new_order_successfully():
    mock_payment_gateway = Mock()
    mock_inventory_service = Mock()
    processor = OrderProcessor(mock_payment_gateway, mock_inventory_service)

    order_details = {"order_id": "ORD001", "items": [{"product_id": "P001", "quantity": 2}], "total_amount": 200.00}

    confirmation = processor.process_order(order_details)

    assert confirmation["status"] == "confirmed"
    assert confirmation["order_id"] == "ORD001"
    mock_payment_gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(200.00)
    mock_inventory_service.deduct_stock.assert_called_once_with("P001", 2)
This test names the API and interactions. Notice how constructor injection and collaborator method names are determined by the assertions.
Teaching points
  • Tests define the constructor signature by showing which dependencies must exist.
  • Asserting calls on mocks clarifies collaborator APIs and interaction patterns.
  • Avoid asserting internal state; prefer observable results and interactions.
Misconception

Asserting private internals can lock you into brittle designs. Test the observable contract instead.

screens.title: Constructor Injection and Collaborators
screens.narratorSegment: When a test constructs an object with mock dependencies it intentionally shapes the class architecture. Constructor injection makes collaborators explicit and testable. In the OrderProcessor example, providing a payment gateway and inventory service in the constructor clarifies responsibilities: the processor coordinates payment and stock changes, but it does not implement charging or stock management itself. This separation reduces coupling, enables mocking in tests, and keeps each class focused on one purpose. A common misconception is that constructor injection is verbose; in practice it simplifies testing and signals design boundaries clearly. Another design insight tests reveal is interaction ordering: the test asserts charge is called and then deduct_stock, which encourages you to think about transactional concerns. If a failure can occur after charging, tests will prompt you to design a rollback or transaction manager. As a takeaway, ask yourself: which collaborators should be passed in so you can mock external effects in tests? Constructor Injection and Collaborators means pass collaborators into constructors so tests can mock interactions and classes stay focused on coordination, not implementation.. In practical terms, why the test suggests passing dependencies to the constructor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Constructor Injection
Architecture

Explicit dependencies for testability

Constructor injection makes collaborators visible and mockable. It separates coordination from implementation and keeps classes single-purpose.
Concrete effect
Mocks let tests assert that charge and deduct_stock were called, which clarifies the interaction contract.
Design question
If an operation can fail mid-way, should you introduce a TransactionManager? Tests will show you when.
Example
class OrderProcessor:
  def __init__(self, payment_gateway, inventory_service):
    self._payment_gateway = payment_gateway
    self._inventory_service = inventory_service

  def process_order(self, order_details: dict) -> dict:
    # minimal implementation to satisfy tests
    self._payment_gateway.charge(order_details["total_amount"])
    for item in order_details["items"]:
      self._inventory_service.deduct_stock(item["product_id"], item["quantity"])
    return {"status": "confirmed", "order_id": order_details["order_id"]}
Key Takeaway

Constructor injection keeps responsibilities clear and enables tests to drive interaction contracts.

screens.title: Implementing the Minimal Code
screens.narratorSegment: In the Green phase you implement the minimum required to make the test pass. The goal is not elegance but correctness with the least amount of code. In our OrderProcessor example that means calling the payment gateway with the order total, deducting stock for each item, and returning a confirmation dictionary. This minimal approach keeps the implementation straightforward and prevents premature abstraction. A common trap is to refactor too early or add features that aren't requested by tests. After the test is green, you have two choices: leave the code as a working stub, or refactor to improve clarity and remove duplication. Tests provide the safety net for refactoring. A concrete example of minimal code is a simple process_order that iterates items, calls deduct_stock, and returns a small confirmation. The closing question is: which parts of your minimal implementation are implementation details that tests should not lock you into? Implementing the Minimal Code means implement only what the test requires; delay abstractions until tests indicate them.. In practical terms, turn the failing test green with the smallest possible implementation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Green Phase — Minimal Code
Minimal implementation
# order_processor.py
class OrderProcessor:
    def __init__(self, payment_gateway, inventory_service):
        self._payment_gateway = payment_gateway
        self._inventory_service = inventory_service

    def process_order(self, order_details: dict) -> dict:
        # Minimal code to pass the test
        self._payment_gateway.charge(order_details["total_amount"])
        for item in order_details["items"]:
            self._inventory_service.deduct_stock(item["product_id"], item["quantity"])
        return {"status": "confirmed", "order_id": order_details["order_id"]}
Teaching notes
  • Minimal implementations reduce risk and keep focus on specified behavior.
  • Avoid adding exception handling or abstractions until tests require them.
  • After green, plan refactors that improve clarity without changing behavior.
Reflection

Which lines in your minimal implementation are likely candidates for extraction once several tests need similar logic?

screens.title: Refactoring to Improve Design
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring is where TDD's design benefits actually appear. Once tests are green, you can safely change names, extract classes, and introduce domain types because tests ensure behavior remains correct. In the OrderProcessor flow you might spot that order_details as a dictionary is error-prone; a test that needs fields across many scenarios will push you to introduce an Order data class. Likewise, repeated patterns for payment or inventory calls suggest introducing a TransactionManager or explicit collaborator interfaces. A critical refactoring driver is a failing test that requires semantics not currently expressed; that test reveals a missing abstraction. A typical pitfall is skipping refactoring; without it your codebase accumulates technical debt. Another is refactoring internals while tests assert private details — tests should express observable behavior to avoid brittleness. Close with a practical question: which repeated pattern in your code should your next refactor extract? Refactoring to Improve Design means use the green test as a safety net to extract clear abstractions and domain types when tests demand them.. In practical terms, when and how to extract abstractions, types, and error handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Refactor Phase
Refactor opportunities
Domain object
Replace loose dictionaries with an Order class when multiple tests need structured access.
Transaction handling
If charge can succeed and stock deduction fail, tests will prompt a rollback or transaction manager.
Extract collaborator interfaces
Make clear interfaces for payment and inventory services to simplify testing and future implementations.
Refactor checklist
  • Does a repeated pattern appear in three or more places?
  • Are tests fragile because they inspect internals?
  • Can names be improved to make intent clearer?
Key Takeaway

Refactor after green; let tests guide extraction of domain types and transaction concerns so design improves incrementally.

screens.title: Emergent Design vs. Big-Bang Design
screens.narratorSegment: Emergent design is a natural outcome of practicing TDD. Rather than attempting to predict every future requirement and building a complex architecture up front, emergent design grows as tests reveal needed behavior. In big-bang design you might spend time crafting abstractions for features that never arrive. Tests-first prevents over-design because you implement only what current tests demand. A concrete contrast: building a full transaction manager before seeing a single failure case is costly if you never need it, whereas adding it after a test demonstrates a failure case is efficient and well-justified. A common mistake is mistaking emergent design for laziness — it is not. It is a disciplined, evidence-based approach that lets structure be added when it is warranted by tests. To practice this, ask: which part of your codebase looks like premature architecture and can wait until a test requires it? Emergent Design vs. Big-Bang Design means emergent design avoids wasted effort by adding complexity only when tests reveal a real need.. Big-Bang Design
Predicts future needs, builds complex abstractions upfront, risks wasted work.
Emergent Design

Emergent design still requires discipline: write clear tests, refactor thoughtfully, and extract abstractions when multiple tests demand the same structure.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How Tests Protect Design
screens.narratorSegment: TDD can fail to improve design when common mistakes creep in. One mistake is skipping the refactor stage; without it tests verify behavior but the codebase remains messy. Another is writing tests that couple to implementation details — private variables or internal helper calls — which makes tests brittle and blocks refactoring. A third is over-design during the red phase: anticipating future needs and adding complexity that tests do not require. Tests protect you only if they express the public contract and if you refactor after green. Use tests to assert outputs and interactions, not private state. When you need to change internals, update tests to reflect the contract, not how the contract is achieved. A practical tip: write tests as examples of usage. If a change improves clarity but keeps the same contract, your tests should still pass. End by asking: which of these mistakes are you most likely to make, and how will you prevent it? Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on: NotificationService
Starter test example
# test_notification_service.py
from notification_service import NotificationService
from unittest.mock import Mock

def test_send_email_notification():
    mock_email_sender = Mock()
    service = NotificationService(mock_email_sender)

    service.send_email_notification('user@example.com', 'Hello', 'Welcome')

    mock_email_sender.send.assert_called_once_with('user@example.com', 'Hello', 'Welcome')
Activity steps
  1. Red: write failing test for email sending with an EmailSender mock.
  2. Green: implement minimal NotificationService and EmailSender to pass.
  3. Refactor: add type hints, docstrings, and consider generalizing to multiple senders.
  4. Repeat for SMS channel and then refactor toward a dispatcher only if tests show repetition.
Pro-tip

Write each test to be an example of intended usage. That makes your tests read like documentation for the API you are designing.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll discover how test-driven development becomes a design discipline rather than only a verification tool. By writing tests first, you think like a client: you define how code must behave before choosing internal structures. This outside-in stance forces you to name methods, define parameters, and specify return values in ways that are intuitive for future users of the code. We'll follow concrete examples, including an OrderProcessor that starts as a failing test, moves to a minimal implementation, and then evolves through intentional refactoring. You'll see how each failing test reveals necessary dependencies, constructor shape, and interactions with collaborators such as payment or inventory services. Beyond a single example, we'll explore emergent design: how small tests lead to new classes or abstractions only when truly needed. We'll also highlight common pitfalls like testing implementation details or skipping refactoring, and explain why avoiding those mistakes matters. Finally, a hands-on activity will guide you to design a NotificationService via Red-Green-Refactor, so you can practice letting tests drive your A P I decisions. By the end you should be able to let tests safely steer A P I and class structure without over-design. What design question will your first test force you to answer?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how writing tests first shapes APIs and class structures. This includes describing outside-in design: starting from the client’s view of behavior and letting tests name methods and parameters. You will demonstrate, through examples, how writing a failing test forces the constructor shape and required collaborators, and how subsequent tests reveal new responsibilities. You will also identify opportunities for emergent design: recognizing when a raw data structure should become a domain object or when a new collaborator is needed. Finally, you will understand the role of refactoring backed by tests: why it is the phase where structural quality improves and how tests provide the safety net to evolve code without fear of regression. Each objective pairs a skill with a practical reason why it matters in real projects, and you will practice these skills in a guided activity to solidify the learning.

These objectives emphasize practice and judgment. First, you will write tests that act like a first consumer of your code. That habit forces A P I design decisions you would otherwise leave unexamined. As you add tests, you'll learn to notice when a simple function needs to become a small domain object or when two responsibilities should split into separate classes. Third, you'll practice constructor injection and collaboration through mockable dependencies so that your class boundaries are explicit and testable. Finally, you will adopt disciplined refactoring: after making a test pass you will improve names, extract classes, and remove duplication with confidence because the tests verify external behavior. Each objective ties directly to a short hands-on task where you write failing tests, implement minimal code, and refactor under test coverage so you leave the chapter with both knowledge and muscle memory.

Test-driven development is often presented as a testing technique, but its deeper value is as a design discipline. The central claim is simple: when you write a test before code, you are forced to think about the desired behavior from the consumer’s perspective. That consumer view clarifies what methods should be named, which parameters are necessary, and what a sensible return value looks like. For example, a test that calls process_order forces you to design an OrderProcessor class and to decide whether the class should accept dependencies via its constructor. That single choice already separates concerns: payment and inventory interactions become collaborators rather than hidden internals. A common misconception is that tests only verify correctness; in practice, they reveal A P I shape and surface design smells early. Tests that are hard to write often indicate awkward APIs, which suggests a need to redesign for usability. To practice this definition, treat tests as client code: write them in a way you would like other engineers to call your A P I. A good closing question is: what client behaviors should your next test make obvious?

Outside-in design is the habit of starting from observable behavior and working inward toward implementation. In TDD, the red test is the outside voice: it says what it expects from the system. By asking "How would I use this?" you force decisions about public A P I shape. For instance, choosing whether OrderProcessor accepts raw dictionaries or an Order object, or whether dependencies are passed in the constructor, is prompted by the test. A concrete example: your first failing test might construct OrderProcessor with two mocks and call process_order. That test establishes the constructor signature and the method name before any implementation exists. A common misconception is to assume outside-in prevents low-level design; instead it delays those details until the tests indicate them. The practical result is smaller, more focused classes, and clearer responsibilities. As you add failing tests one by one, the A P I stabilizes and you gain a roadmap for refactoring.
